penalties_applied.name: b2c_at_scale_needed
penalties_applied.reason: Individual developers paying ~$5-10/mo for a browser extension or email plugin requires hundreds to thousands of paying users to generate meaningful revenue; the business model structurally depends on consumer-scale volume.

rationale: The buyer is an individual software engineer — a consumer, not a business with a budget line — and one explicit 'I would pay' from a single HN commenter is a weak commercial signal at scale. While the pain is real and recurring (daily inbox noise), the tool would need hundreds of paying solo users to matter economically, and buyer_clarity is below the build_gate floor of 6. The space is crowded with free Gmail filters, SaneBox, and native Outlook rules, making willingness-to-pay hard to extract above $5-10/mo without a clear differentiation moat.
solution_plan: The micro-service would be a browser extension or Gmail add-on that uses a Claude prompt to classify and score incoming recruiter emails (real vs. AI-generated spray-and-pray) and auto-labels or archives low-score ones. The factory builds it by writing the classification prompt, generating a Chrome Manifest V3 extension scaffold, and setting up a Stripe payment link for a $7/mo subscription — no coding by Youval. To sell, the factory would draft cold posts for HN 'Show HN', r/cscareerquestions, and targeted Twitter/X threads; outreach goes out only after Youval approves each batch. Delivery is fully automated once installed; support is handled by Claude responding to a support email alias. The hard reality: acquiring enough individual-developer subscribers to clear even $1k MRR requires a viral or SEO distribution engine that a solo operator without a public profile will struggle to build — this is a consumer app problem, not a B2B tool problem, so consider dropping unless a specific niche (e.g., Hebrew-speaking Israeli tech workers) can be targeted more precisely.
notes: buyer_clarity (5) is below the build_gate floor of 6. b2c_at_scale_needed penalty applied. The 'I would pay' signal is genuine but isolated; no evidence of a reachable cohort willing to pay at SaaS prices.
